# Manufacturing systems

Relevant for the mechatronics point of view

## Manufacturing systems

![](images-1/technologies.jpg)

To give shape to a block of raw material (*workpiece*) there are three possibilities:

- Deform it: **forming processes** (motion axes: 1+)
- Cut it: material removal (or **subtractive**) processes (motion axes: 2.5+)
- Build on it: **additive manufacturing** processes (motion axes: 2.5+)

## Manufacturing systems

![](images-1/technologies.jpg)

- We skip over forming processes, where motion planning and control is trivial (with exceptions!)
- In subtractive and additive manufacturing there is a tool performing the process (a mill, a polarized wire, an extruding nozzle, ...), whose motion is performed by synchronized action of two or more axes, typically in cartesian arrangement
- The motion (trajectory and speed) must be planned according to geometry and process specifics

## Reference case: Turning/Milling

- The majority of products involve machining, either directly, or indirectly (dies are machined)
- Machining involves a combination of linear and rotary motions:
  - In **turning**, the workpiece is rotating, the tool is displacing
  - In **drilling and milling** the tool is rotating and there is a combined relative displacement between tool and workpiece


::: {.callout-important}

Regardless the process, understanding its physics and the governing parameters is essential to design the manufacturing system and its control algorithms

:::


# The subtractive manufactiring case

Material removal processes and their control parameters

## Machining parameters

- Mechanism of **chip formation** depends
  - on the relative speed of tool and workpiece (**cutting speed**)
  - on the *cross section* of removed material
- Cutting speed and cross section (**tool** parameters) depend in turn on trajectory, rotary and translation speeds (**machining** parameters)

## Turning

Machining parameters to be calculated are **spindle speed**, **feed rate**, and **spindle power**:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Rotational speed:}\quad & N = \frac{v}{\pi D_0} \\
\text{Diameter:}\quad & D_f = D_0 - 2d \\
\text{Feed rate:}\quad & f = N f_r \\
\text{Machining time:}\quad & T_m = \frac{L}{f} = \frac{\pi D_0 L}{f_r v} \\
\text{Material Removal Rate:}\quad & MRR = v f_r d
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](images-1/turning.jpg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::
::::

## Drilling

Machining parameters to be calculated are **spindle speed**, **feed rate**, and **spindle power**:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
N &= \frac{v}{\pi D} \\
f &= N f_r \\
T_m &= \frac{t + A}{f} \\
A &= \frac{D}{2}\tan\left(\frac{\pi - \theta}{2}\right) \\
MRR &= \frac{\pi D^2 f}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](images-1/drilling.jpg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::
::::

## Milling

Machining parameters to be calculated are **spindle speed**, **feed rate**, and **spindle power**. There are three types of milling:

![](images-1/milling.jpg){fig-align="center" height=400}

## Milling

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
N &= \frac{v}{\pi D} \\
f &= N f_z z \\
MRR &= w d f \\
A &= \begin{cases} \sqrt{d(D-d)} & \text{side milling} \\ \sqrt{w(D-w)} & \text{face/end milling} \end{cases} \\
T_m &= \begin{cases} (L + A)/f & \text{side milling} \\ (L + 2A)/f & \text{face/end milling} \end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images-1/milling.jpg){fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

## Shopfloor formulas

| Parameter | Turning | Milling | Drilling |
|:--|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| $v$ (m/min) | $v = \pi D_0 N$ | $v = \pi D N$ | $v = \pi D N$ |
| $N$ (1/s) | $N = \dfrac{v}{\pi D_0}$ | $N = \dfrac{v}{\pi D}$ | $N = \dfrac{v}{\pi D}$ |
| $f$ (mm/min) | $f = f_r N$ | $f = z f_z N$ | $f = f_r N$ |
| $f_{z,r}$ (mm) | *Feed per tooth (zahn) or per revolution* | | |
| $T$ (s) | $T_m = L/f$ | $T_m = (L + kA)/f$ | $T_m = L/f$ |
| $MRR$ (mm³/min) | $MRR = d f_r v$ | $MRR = w d f$ | $MRR = \dfrac{\pi D^2}{4} f$ |
| $P$ (kW) | $P = MRR\, p_s$ | $P = MRR\, p_s$ | $P = MRR\, p_s$ |
| $P_e$ (kW) | $P_e = \dfrac{MRR\, p_s}{\eta}$ | $P_e = \dfrac{MRR\, p_s}{\eta}$ | $P_e = \dfrac{MRR\, p_s}{\eta}$ |

: {.striped}

## Example

We have to set up a milling process on Aluminum, which has $p_s = 12.56$ W min/cm³

The tool manufacturer suggests $v = 1000$ m/min and $f_z = 0.1$ mm/tooth

The mill has a diameter of $30$ mm and does face milling with **full overlapping**, has $3$ teeth and removes a layer of $2$ mm

$$
\begin{aligned}
N &= \frac{v}{\pi D} = \frac{1000\ \text{m/min}}{\pi\, 30\ \text{mm}} = 10610\ \text{rpm} \\
f &= f_z z N = 0.1\ \text{mm} \cdot 3 \cdot 10610\ \text{rpm} = 3183\ \text{mm/min} \\
MRR &= w d f = 30\ \text{mm} \cdot 2\ \text{mm} \cdot 3183\ \text{mm/min} = 190980\ \text{mm}^3/\text{min} \\
P &= MRR\, p_s = 190.98\ \text{cm}^3/\text{min} \cdot 12.56\ \text{W min/cm}^3 \simeq 2.4\ \text{kW}
\end{aligned}
$$


::: {.callout-note}
The machininst must always ensure that the required maximum power does not exceet that available at the spindle. If not, some of the machining parameters must be reduced (usually $d$ and or $w$)
:::


## Cutting Economics

The cost of machining depends on:

- **labor:** hourly cost of trained personnel
- **machinery:** purchase cost / machine life
- **raw material:** cost of initial workpiece
- **consumables:** tools, cutting fluids, disposable fixtures

Some costs depend on process parameters (mainly cutting speed)

## Tool wear

![](images-1/tool-wear.png){fig-align="center" height=500}

## Tool wear

Tools are subject to **wear**. It can affect two parts of the tool:

-   the [flank]{.bred}: it changes the geometry of the tool where it
    contacts the workpiece, so it progressively affects surface quality
    and dimensional accuracy
-   the [rake face]{.bblue}: it changes the geometry where the tool
    contacts the chip: it has no effect on the workpiece, but in the
    long run it weakens the tool and causes it to break

If the tool and the cutting parameters are chosen correctly, flank
wear occurs before rake face wear

The wear law was formulated by Taylor: $VT^n=K$, where:


-   $V$ is the cutting speed
-   $T$ is the tool life
-   $n$ and $K$ are material constants; $K$ also depends on the
    **end-of-life criterion** (application specific)

## Taylor's law

$VT^n=K \rightarrow \log(V) - n\log(T) = \log(K) \rightarrow \log(T) = \frac{1}{n}\log(V) - \frac{1}{n}\log(K)$

::::: columns
::: column
```{r}
set.seed(0)
wc <- 200
round_next <- function(x, d) round(x/d) * d
w <- function(t,v, k=0.2, a=10) a*v^(k*t)
life <- function(v, wmax, k=0.2) uniroot(\(x) w(x, v, k) - wmax, interval=c(0, 1e5))$root
vels <- c(5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 40)

df <- expand.grid(
  T = seq(2, 10, length.out=50),
  V = vels
) %>%
  mutate(w = w(T, V, k=0.3)) %>% 
  mutate(w = round_next(w, 5)) %>% 
  filter(w <= wc + 30) 

df_l <- df %>% 
  filter(w <= wc) %>% 
  group_by(V) %>% 
  summarise(T = T[which.max(w)], w=max(w))

df %>% 
  mutate(V=factor(V)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=T, y=w, group=V, color=V)) + 
  geom_point(data=df_l, aes(x=T, y=w), color="red", shape=4, size=5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=wc, color="red", linetype=2) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_viridis_d(breaks=vels) +
  labs(x="Time (min)", y="Wear (µm)", title="Interrupted cutting experiments")
```
:::

::: column
```{r}
df_l %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=log(V), y=log(T))) +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", formula=y~x) +
  geom_point() + 
  labs(title = "Taylor's law")
```
:::
:::::

## Productivity optimization

The costs of machining production are related to:

-   investments and *overhead* ([fixed]{.rbold})
-   labor and raw materials ([variable]{.rgreen})
-   cost per piece ([variable]{.rgreen})

Costs are dependent variables. The process parameters are
**independent parameters**

::: callout-important
We can ask whether there are process conditions that
[maximize]{.bgreen} productivity and/or [minimize]{.bred} costs
:::

## Productivity optimization --- Turning

::::: columns
:::{.column .smaller width="30%"}
| Symbol  | Meaning           |
|---------|-------------------|
| $C_p$   | Cost per piece    |
| $C_m$   | Machining cost    |
| $C_s$   | Setup cost        |
| $C_l$   | Loading cost      |
| $C_t$   | Tooling cost      |
| $L$     | Labor cost        |
| $O$     | Overhead          |

In **turning**:
$$
T_m = \frac{L}{fN}=\frac{\pi LD}{fV} \\
N_p = \frac{T}{T_m} = \frac{fK^{1/n}}{\pi LDV^{1/n-1}}
$$
:::

:::{.column width="70%"}
\begin{align}
C_p &= C_m + C_s + C_l + C_t \\
C_m &= T_m(L_m + O_m) \\
C_l &= T_l(L_m + O_m) \\
C_t &= \frac{1}{N_p}\left[T_c(L_m+O_m) + T_g(L_g+O_g) + D_c\right] = \frac{C_{t0}}{N_p} \\
T_p &= T_{s,l} + T_m + \frac{C_{t0}}{N_p}
\end{align}

:::callout-note
We have $C_p=C_p(V)$ and $T_p = T_p(V)$, so we can differentiate both to identify an optimal condition
:::
:::
:::


## Productivity optimization --- Turning

:::columns
:::column
**Costs**:
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial C_p}{\partial V} &= 0 \\
V_{o,c} &= \frac{K(L_m+O_m)^n}{[(1/n-1)C_{t0}]^n} \\
T_{o,c} &= (1/n -1)\frac{C_{t0}}{L_m+O_m}
\end{align}
:::

:::column
**Times**:
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial T_p}{\partial V} &= 0 \\
V_{o,t} &= \frac{K}{[(1/n-1)T_c]^n} \\
T_{0,t} &= (1/n -1)T_c
\end{align}
:::
:::

:::callout-note
What do we optimize? Costs or times?
:::

## Productivity optimization --- Turning

:::columns
:::column
* The optimal cutting speed $V_{o,c}$ corresponds to maximum economic efficiency
* However, when there are **penalties for delays** it may be worth producing at $V_{o,t}$, because it is the speed that **maximizes productivity**
* So, $V$ shall be normally set to $V_{o,c}$, increasing it up to (but not above) $V_{o,t}$ if there are penalties for delays
:::

:::column
```{r}
L <- 100
D <- 50
f <- 0.5
Lm <- 1
Om <- 0.7
Cs <- 1
Cl <- 1
K <- 50
n <- 0.5
Ct0 <- 2
Cs <- 10*(Lm + Om)
Cl <- 100*(Lm + Om)
Tm <- function(V) (pi * L * D) / (f*V)
Np <- function(V) (K/V)^(1/n)/Tm(V)
Ct <- function(V) Ct0/Np(V)
Cm <- function(V) Tm(V) * (Lm + Om)

Voc <- (K*(Lm+Om)^n)/((1/n-1)*Ct0)^n
Vot <- K/((1/n-1)*0.5)^n

tibble(
  V = seq(10, 300, length.out=100),
  Cs = Cs,
  Cl = Cl,
  Cm = Cm(V),
  Ct = Ct(V),
  Cp = Cm + Ct + Cs + Cl
) %>% 
  pivot_longer(-V, names_to = "Item", values_to = "Cost") %>% 
  mutate(Cost = Cost/70) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=V)) + 
  geom_line(aes(y=Cost, color=Item)) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept=c(Voc, Vot), linetype=2, color="red") + 
  ylim(c(0, 60)) + 
  labs(x="Cutting speed (m/min)", y="Cost (€)")
```
:::
:::


## Limits of analytical process models

### Orthogonal cutting

* Orthogonal cutting **rarely applies**. In most real machining operations chip formation is inherently 3-D
* The chip formation model is idealized. In reality:
  - the cutting edge is never perfectly sharp
  - the shear plane does not have zero thickness
  - deformation does not occur only on the shear plane, but also on the machined surface in contact with the cutting edge and between chip and tool
* The stress and strain field cannot be computed analytically
* There is no reliable **thermal model** that accounts for friction and plastic deformation as heat sources
* The strain rates involved $\dot\gamma$ are extreme: this makes it very difficult to identify the plastic properties of the material under similar conditions


## Limits of analytical process models
### Taylor's law

* It is an **empirical model**, i.e., it has no physical basis but rests on observation alone, so it cannot be calibrated from measurements of material properties
* It is an approximate law: more complete empirical laws exist in the form $VT^nd^xf^y=K$, which account for other process parameters that have a much smaller influence than $V$ but still affect tool life
* It is **expensive** to calibrate:
  - the experimental procedure is necessarily slow and costly
  - $n$ depends on the workpiece material and on the tool material
  - $K$ depends on the **end-of-life criterion**, so it is user-specific (i.e., it cannot be found in tables)
* Even the more complete laws do not account for factors such as **lubrication and cooling**


## Economic optimization

* The analysis above depends on being able to **express $T_m(V)$ analytically**
  - This is possible **only for elementary operations** (e.g., cylindrical turning). For more complex operations the relation can only be computed point by point by simulating the process (via CAM or CNC functions, which entails **considerable time and cost**)
  - It relies on the availability of a validated and reliable wear law
  - It is worthwhile only for large and very large batches (economy of scale)

:::
::::

## CNC lathe

- A lathe with enhanced motion controller (**Computer-Numerical-Controller**, CNC)
- Mechanical layout is arranged in order to allow automated chip evacuation
- 3 controlled axes + spindle, or more
- The spindle can be a controlled axis itself
- It can have rotary tools, too (hybrid turning-milling)

- Roller-turner (revolving) turret
- Counterstock (hydraulics)
- Inclined bed
- Lead screw

## Universal milling center


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

* Universl milling centers have a **rotary table** and a **universal milling head** that can be tilted and swiveled to machine any surface of the workpiece
* By rotating the axis at 45° from Z, the spindle axis can be changed from vertical to horizontal (*universal*)

:::

::: {.column}
![Universal milling head](images-1/universal-head.jpg){fig-align="center" height=400}
:::

:::



## Architectures

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Cantilever:** simplest and cheapest
- **Traveling column:** suitable when one axis is much longer
- **Gantry:** much more stiff and stable, but more complex (twin axes)
- **Parallel-K:** much stiffer and faster, but complex to control and limited in travels
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/architectures.jpg){fig-align="center" height=330}
:::
::::

## Vertical spindle

:::columns
:::column
[Pros]{.bgreen}:

- Easy fixturing
- Reduced moveable mass

**Cons**:

- Chip disposal is more difficult
- Not suitable for machinind dies/cavities
:::

:::column
![Vertical spindle machine](images-1/vertical-spindle.jpg)
:::
:::

## Horizontal spindle

:::columns
:::column
[Pros]{.bgreen}:

- Better chip/liquids disposal
- Large travels

**Cons**:

- More difficult fixturing
- More moveable mass (slower)
- more difficult to fixture
:::

:::column
![Horizontal spindle machine](images-1/horizontal-spindle.png)
:::
:::

## Pallet changer

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="35%"}
- Stocky WPs
- High productivity
- can be integrated in automated lines
:::
::: {.column width="65%"}
![Pallet changer](images-1/pallet-changer-machine.png)
:::
::::

## Traveling column

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Suitable for:

- slender WP
- stocky WP but with two alternating fixturing zones (higher productivity)


::: {.callout-important}
### Masked time

Any operation that can be performed in parallel to machining is said to happen in *masked time*. It's cost is absorbed in the machining cost

Other operations happen in *exposed time*, which is added to the machining cost

:::

# Automation

*It is mainly a matter of synchronizing motion*

![](images/automation-photo.jpg){fig-align="center" height=320}

## Amber & Amber {.smaller}

*The Yardstick of Automation* (1962)

| Order | Human attribute | Example |
|:-:|:-:|:--|
| 0 | None | Utensili manuali |
| 1 | Energy | Powered machines and tools |
| 2 | Dexterity | Single-cycle automatics (*dexterity = self-feeding*) |
| 3 | Diligence | Repeats cycle; open-loop control |
| 4 | Judgment | Closed loop; numerical control; self-measuring |
| 5 | Evaluation | Computer control; model of process required for automation |
| 6 | Learning | Limited self-programming; some artificial intelligence |
| 7 | Reasoning | Inductive reasoning (cause-effects) |
| 8 | Creativity | Performs (original) design unaided |
| 9 | Dominance | Machine is master (HAL 9000) |

: {.striped .hover}

## Current level: A(4)

  - Convert a machining description in machining movements

## Drivers

![](images-1/driver-loop.svg){fig-align="center" height=140}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
Requirements:

- Fast response (acceleration)
- Quick stabilization (minimum number of oscillations)
- **No overshoot** (or risk of damages)
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| out-width: "443px"
#| out-height: "290px"
#| fig-align: center
# P-controlled position loop, G(s) = k / (s (tau s + 1)): closed-loop step response
step_response <- function(t, Kp, k = 34.7, tau = 0.02) {
  wn <- sqrt(Kp * k / tau)
  zeta <- 1 / (2 * sqrt(Kp * k * tau))
  wd <- wn * sqrt(1 - zeta^2)
  1 - exp(-zeta * wn * t) * (cos(wd * t) + zeta / sqrt(1 - zeta^2) * sin(wd * t))
}
expand_grid(t = seq(0, 0.2, length.out = 500), Kp = c(1, 11, 21)) %>%
  mutate(theta = step_response(t, Kp), Kp = factor(Kp)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = t, y = theta, color = Kp)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Position (rad)", color = quote(K[p]))
```
:::

## PLC: Programmable Logic Controller

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
PLC is a controller taht implemets logic relationships between inputs and outputs. It provides a range of interfaces and registers:

- Analog and digital I/O (> 2048)
- Relay (1000)
- Memories (200)
- Timers (200)
- Counters (200)

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images-1/cnc-block-diagram.svg){fig-align="center" height=430}
:::
::::


::: {.callout-note}
Can be either a separate hardware, or a software process running on the same computer that runs the CNC
:::


## PLC

* Beside GPIO, PLC can also have advanced I/O and communication capabilities:
  - General purpose communication: RS232, RS422, Ethernet
  - Deterministic communication: Profibus, DeviceNet, Modbus, Industrial EtherNET, CAN-BUS
  - Special I/O: counters, virtual cams, PIDs and controllers
* PLC programming languages have been designed to facilitate the transition form **wired logics** to **software logics**: the languages had to be intuitive and immediately productive for technicians with different backgrounds: **electrical engineering**, control engineering, firmware programming

## PLC

The programming standard **IEC 61131-3** provided this transition:

| Language | Type | Description |
| ----- |:-:| --------- |
| Ladder Logic | Graphical | Resembles relay logic diagrams, intuitive for electricians |
| Function Block Diagram | Graphical | Resembles block diagrams, intuitive for control engineers |
| Sequential Function Chart | Graphical | Resembles flow charts and [finite state machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite-state_machine), intuitive for process engineers |
| Structured Text | Textual | Resembles Pascal, intuitive for software engineers |
| Instruction List | Textual | Resembles assembly, intuitive for firmware engineers |


::: {.callout-note}
The standard states that languages must be interchangeable, i.e., the same program can be written in any language and must have the same behavior, different parts of a program can be written in different languages, and the program can be converted from one language to another
:::


## PLC: Ladder diagram

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}

::: {.callout-note}
* On the left side there are **contactors** (inputs), on the right side there are **coils** (outputs).
* parallel branches represent **OR** logic, series branches represent **AND** logic; contactors can be **normally open** or **normally closed** (**NOT**).
* The program is read from left to right, top to bottom. The program is executed in a **cyclic scan**: all inputs are read, the logic is evaluated, and the outputs are updated.
:::

:::

::: {.column width="70%"}
![](images-1/plc-ladder.svg){fig-align="center" height=470}
:::
:::



## PLC: Function Block Diagram

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
::: {.callout-note}
* Each block implements a function, which can be a logic function, a timer, a counter, or even a more complicated one as a PID controller
* Appeals to control engineers, being quite similar to [Simulink](https://www.mathworks.com/products/simulink.html) and other block-diagram-based control design software
* Complex programs tend to become quite messy, so FBD is often used in combination with other languages and limited to implement specific functions related to control and signal processing
:::
:::

::: {.column width="70%"}
![](images-1/plc-fbd.svg){fig-align="center" height=470}
:::
:::




## PLC: Sequential Function Chart
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
::: {.callout-note}
* SFC is a graphical language that implements a **finite state machine**
* Each block is a **state**, each line a transition with its activation condition
*  It is very intuitive for process engineers, and it is often used in combination with other languages to implement the **overall logic** of a process, while the other languages are used to implement the **details** of each state
:::
:::

::: {.column width="70%"}
![](images-1/plc-sfc.svg){fig-align="center" height=470}
:::
:::

## PLC: Textual languages

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{.pascal filename="Structured Text (ST)" code-line-numbers="false"}
(* motor start/stop with seal-in *)
Motor := (Start_PB OR Motor)
         AND NOT Stop_PB
         AND NOT Overload;
Inlet_Valve := Motor AND NOT Level_Hi;
T1(IN := Motor, PT := T#10s);
IF T1.Q THEN
  Run_Lamp := TRUE;
END_IF;
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{.asm filename="Instruction List (IL)" code-line-numbers="false"}
LD   Start_PB
OR   Motor
ANDN Stop_PB
ANDN Overload
ST   Motor
LD   Motor
ANDN Level_Hi
ST   Inlet_Valve
CAL  T1(IN := Motor, PT := T#10s)
LD   T1.Q
S    Run_Lamp
```
:::
::::


::: {.callout-note}
Textual languages are the most easy to implement and always available even on low-cost PLC and PLC IDEs
:::


## (Computer) Numerical Control

The CNC controller is the **brain** of the machine tool. It implements the **judgement** (A4) of Amber's scale, and it is responsible for:

* parsing the **part-program**
* converting it into **motion commands** for the machine tool actuators
* provinding action inputs to the **PLC controller** for auxiliary functions (coolant, tool change rutines, etc.)

CNC controllers are characterized by:

- Types of **motion interpolation**
- Number of **controlled axes**


## Types of motion interpolation

CNC can control axes with increasing levels of sophistication:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .smaller width="40%"}
- **Point to point**: only the start and end points are controlled, the path is not controlled (drilling, pick-and-place)
- **Paraxial**: one axis at a time can be **controlled in feed** (semi-automatic machines, machines that don't need axes interpolation as sawing machines, presses)
- [Continuous]{.bgreen}: all axes can be controlled simultaneously, and the path is controlled in position and velocity
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
<iframe data-src="images-1/scenes.html#interp" title="3D view, drag to rotate" style="width:100%; height:430px; border:none;"></iframe>
:::
::::

## Number of controlled axes

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- 2 Axes: third axis is manually adjusted (manual lathes, manual mills)
- 2 Axes and 1/2: only two axes at a time can be controlled, the third is for positioning
- 3 Axes: full 3-D trajectory control of TCP
- 5 Axes: full trajectory control of TCP and tool orientation
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
<iframe data-src="images-1/scenes.html#axes" title="3D view, drag to rotate" style="width:100%; height:450px; border:none;"></iframe>
:::
::::

## Coordinate systems


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

- Axes references combine to give machine origin
- Axes references are used to reset encoders (*homing*)
- Machine controller works in **machine coordinates**
- Workpiece origin is **set up by the operator**
- Registration point is the reference to measure tool length and diameter
- Support point is the reference to mount the tool on the spindle (when mounted, *reference = support*)


:::

::: {.column}

| Reference | Symbol |
| --------- | :-: |
| Axis reference | ![](images-1/axis-reference.png){fig-align="center" height=30} |
| Machine origin | ![](images-1/machine-origin.png){fig-align="center" height=30} |
| Workpiece origin | ![](images-1/wp-origin.png){fig-align="center" height=30} |
| Registration point | ![](images-1/registration-point.png){fig-align="center" height=30} |
| Support point | ![](images-1/support-point.png){fig-align="center" height=30} |

:::

:::


## Tool reference

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Support point:**
  - Abutment plane (lathes)
  - Spindle nose (mills)
- **Registration point:**
  - on the tool, the point that matches the SP when mounted
- **To be measured:**
  - Length and offset (lathes)
  - Length, diameter, and toric radius (mills)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images-1/tool-ref.svg){fig-align="center" height=450}
:::
::::


## WP coordinates

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
- Selected by operator/programmer
- Part program can use WP coordinates and/or machine coordinates
- After fixturing, WP origin has to be set up wrt machine origin
  - by touching with tool and compensating for tool radius
  - By 3-D touch probe
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
<iframe data-src="images-1/scenes.html#wp" title="3D view, drag to rotate" style="width:100%; height:400px; border:none;"></iframe>
:::
::::


## Coordinate transformations

* The part program defines the toolpath as the trajectory of the **tool center position** (TCP) in the workpiece reference frame
* The CNC controller converts the TCP coordinates into **machine coordinates** by applying a roto-translation transformation that accounts for:
  - the workpiece origin
  - the tool length
* Tool diameter is accounted for by the **tool radius compensation** function, which offsets the toolpath by the tool radius in a direction perpendicular to the toolpath


::: {.callout-note}
In turning, there is no tool radius compensation; rather, tool is measured by **length** and **abuttment**, the latter being the offset w.r.t. the registration point
:::


## Coordinate transformations

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
Any coordinate $P_{wp}$ given in the workpiece reference frame $O_{wp}$ is converted in machine coordinates $P_m$, including tool length offset

$$
P_m = T_{wp \to m} P_{wp}; \qquad
T_{wp \to m} = \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & r_{12} & r_{13} & d_x \\ r_{21} & r_{22} & r_{23} & d_y \\ r_{31} & r_{32} & r_{33} & d_z + l_t \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

$d_{x-z}$ are coordinates of $O_{wp}$ in $O_m$
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images-1/transform-3d.svg){fig-align="center" height=330}
:::
::::

## Coordinate transformations

Remember that the roto-translation matrix is:

$$
T = \begin{bmatrix}
\cos\alpha\cos\beta & \cos\alpha\sin\beta\sin\gamma - \sin\alpha\cos\beta & \cos\alpha\sin\beta\cos\gamma + \sin\alpha\sin\gamma & d_x \\
\sin\alpha\cos\beta & \sin\alpha\sin\beta\sin\gamma + \cos\alpha\cos\beta & \sin\alpha\sin\beta\cos\gamma - \cos\alpha\sin\gamma & d_y \\
-\sin\beta & \cos\beta\sin\gamma & \cos\beta\cos\gamma & d_z \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
The **order of transformations** is:

1. Roll by $\gamma$
2. Pitch by $\beta$
3. Yaw by $\alpha$
4. Translate by $(d_x, d_y, d_z)$
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
![](images-1/rpy.svg){fig-align="center" height=230}
:::
::::


## Coordinate transformations (3-axes machines)

Machines with 3 controlled axes (no tool alignment) typically implement a simplified transformation that only accounts for the workpiece origin translation and rotation $\theta$ about $z$ and tool length:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} x_m \\ y_m \\ z_m \\1 \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 & d_x \\
\sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 & d_y \\
0 & 0 & 1 & d_z + l_t \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.callout-tip title="Workplane tilt compensation"}
Even for 3 axes machines, it is customary to also include **small** rotations about $x$ and $y$ in the transformation matrix, to account for **misalignments** of the working plane and tool holder: this comes especially handy for **3-D printers**
:::





# {background-iframe="MillCoordinates/machine-frames.html" background-interactive="true"}


## Measuring positions: touch probe

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Reference positions (as $O_{wp}$can be measure in machine thanks to a **touch probe**:

- a special non-rotating tool with a deflecting stylus and spherical tip that can be used to touch the workpiece and measure its position in machine coordinates
- The 3 contact points provide a [kinematic mount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinematic_coupling) are also electric switches
- When a switch opens, the current coordinate plus the **sphere radius in the direction of motion** gives the touch point coordinate
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images/touch-probe.jpg){fig-align="center" height=440}
:::
::::


## Tool reference (*presetting*)

Tool geometry can be measured in machine (**exposed time**) or by a **tool presetter** (**masked time**). The latter is preferred because it is faster and more accurate, and it allows to measure the tool geometry without having to mount it on the machine.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="37%"}
- On-board presetting uses a fixed stylus/switched contact point in known position reachable by the tool
- Tool presetting systems have a dummy spindle mount, a camera and a shadow projector
:::
::: {.column width="63%"}
![](images/presetting-1.jpg){fig-align="center" height=250}
![](images/presetting-3.jpg){fig-align="center" height=250}
![](images/presetting-2.jpg){fig-align="center" height=250}
:::
::::

## Automation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
According to the Yardstick of Automation:

- most CNC machines are at Level A4 
- Level A5 requires post-machining automated inspection and feedback to the CNC controller and **to the part-program**
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](images-1/yardstick-loop.svg){fig-align="center" height=280}
:::
::::

- a validated **process model** can be required to implement A5, which is not necessarilyavailable for most machining processes
- empirical models (*machine learning*) can be used to implement A5, but they require a lot of data and are not always reliable

## Machining cycle

The general sequence for machining a part is:

![](images-1/machining-cycle.svg){fig-align="center" height=260}

The section within the red box is the **mcahining cycle**, i.e. the sequence of operations that can be cyclically repeated for each part

## Part-program structure


::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
The structure of a part program generally follows a common structure:

* **setups**
* **roughing** section: removes the bulk of the material, usually with a large tool and high feedrate, leaving a small allowance for finishing
* **finishing** section: removes the remaining material with a small tool and low feedrate (final geometry)
* **reset** of the machine to a safe position and end of program
:::

::: {.column}
![](images-1/part-program.png){fig-align="center" height=490}
:::
:::




## Toolpaths

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
![](images-1/turning-process.png){fig-align="center" height=490}
:::

::: {.column}
* Roughing and finishing may require different tools for different geometries
* Roughing typically follows simple, stepped trajectories 
* Roughing allowance (excess material) is usually in the range of 
  - 0.5--1 mm for turning
  - 0.2--0.5 mm for milling
:::
::::

## Workpiece Origin

In turning, X coordinates are in **diameters**. Two typical choices for origin:

- rightmost axial point on finished workpiece
- on the machine origin (fixtures must be taken into consideration)

Common choice for WP origin among machinists is the **rightmost axial point on finished workpiece** (turning) and **topmost point on the finished workpiece** (milling). This choice allows to quickly spot in a program **safe** fast motions (positive $z$), from **dangerous** fast motions (negative $z$) that can crash the tool into the workpiece or fixture.

## G-Code

**ISO language** (ISO/DIN 6983): sequence of `[C][arg]` where `C` is a letter and `arg` is a number. Valid commands are:


::: {.columns .smaller}

::: {.column}
| Cod. | Command |
| ---- | -------------- |
| A | Rotation about X |
| B | Rotation about Y |
| C | Rotation about Z |
| D | Tool diameter compensation |
| E | Secondary feedrate |
| F | Feedrate |
| G | Preparatory function |
| H | --- |
| I | Circle center, X |
:::

::: {.column}

| Cod. | Command |
| ---- | -------------- |
| J | Circle center, Y |
| K | Circle center, Z |
| L | --- |
| M | Machine function |
| N | Block number |
| O | --- |
| P | Third motion along X |
| Q | Third motion along Y |
|   |  |
:::

::: {.column}


| Cod. | Command |
| - | - |
| R | Third motion along Z |
| S | Spindle speed |
| T | Tool number |
| U | Second motion along X |
| V | Second motion along Y |
| W | Second motion along Z |
| X | Motion along X |
| Y | Motion along Y |
| Z | Motion along Z |

:::

:::




## Punch tape

* [G-Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G-code){target="wiki"} was developed during 1950s
* Computers only had **punch tapes** as input devices
* Language had to be concise

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="35%"}
![](images/punch-tape-photo.jpg){fig-align="center" height=280}
:::
::: {.column width="65%"}
![](images-1/punch-tape.svg){fig-align="center" height=280}
:::
::::


## G-code functions

:::: columns
:::column
Types of functions:

- Preparatory functions (`G`, `T`)
- Positioning functions (`X`, `Y`, `Z`, `A`, `B`, `C`)
- Machine functions (`M`)
:::

:::column
`G` functions:

* `G00`: **rapid positioning**
* `G01`: **linear interpolation**
* `G02/G03`: **circular interpolation** (CW/CCW)
:::
::::

```{.gcode code-line-numbers="false"}
N1 T1 S500.0 M3                             ; tool n°1, CW rotation, 500 rpm
N2 M8;                                      ; fluid jets ON
N3 G00 X60.0 Z0.0;                          ; rapid positioning
N4 G01 X-0.5 Z0.0 F1000.0                   ; facing
N5 G01 X20.0 F1000.0
N6 G03 X40.0 Z-5.0 I30.0 K-10.0 F1000.0     ; arc R=10.0
...
N128 M30                                    ; fine programma
```

## Example: milling


::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
* WP origin is usually placed in $y,y$ plane on a geometry feature where most of the dimensions are referenced to, e.g. the bottom-left corner of a rectangular pocket
* The $z$ coordinate is set to the topmost surface on the **finished part**:
  - the very first roughing operation will remove the excess material and reach the finished surface, which will be used as reference for all subsequent operations
  - any subsequent operation is carried out at a **negative $z$** coordinate, which is the depth of cut below the finished surface

:::

::: {.column}
![](images-1/milling-part.png){fig-align="center" height=480}
:::
:::

## Advanced languages

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
Different CNC manufacturers implement proprietary languages that extend the basic G-code with advanced features:

- Explicit, reacher syntax
- Conversational/interactive programming (*zero-handbook*)
- Macros
- Parametric programming
:::

::: {.column .smaller width="40%"}
```{.gcode filename="Heidenhain language" code-line-numbers="false"}
0  BEGIN PGM es1 MM
1  BLK FORM 0.1 Z  X+0  Y+0  Z-20
2  BLK FORM 0.2  X+150  Y+150  Z+0
3  CYCL DEF 247 DEF. ZERO PEZZO ~
    Q339=+1    ;NUMERO ORIGINE
4  TOOL CALL 1 Z S5000 F4000
5  M8
6  L  X+10  Y-10  Z+10 R0 FMAX
7  L  Z-10 R0 FMAX
8  L  Y+95 RL F AUTO
9  L  X+36  Y+140
10 RND R10 F AUTO
11 L  X+105
12 CHF 4
13 L IY-55
14 RND R14
15 L IX+35
16 RND R5
17 L  X+105  Y+14
18 CHF 8
19 L  X-15
20 L  Z+10 R0 FMAX
21 STOP M30
22 END PGM es1 MM
```

# CNC

*Algorithms for Computer Numerical Control --- machining complex shapes*

![](images/cnc-photo.jpg){fig-align="center" height=300}

```{r}
#| include: false
# Helpers for the profiling and look-ahead plots of this section

# Trapezoidal feed profile of a block on a discrete clock (period tq):
# the block duration is rounded up to a multiple of tq and f_m reduced accordingly
quantize_block <- function(l, fm, a, d, fs, fe, tq) {
  t1 <- (fm - fs) / a
  t2 <- (fm - fe) / d
  tm <- l / fm - t1 * (fm + fs) / (2 * fm) - t2 * (fe + fm) / (2 * fm)
  dt <- t1 + tm + t2
  dts <- (floor(dt / tq) + 1) * tq
  tms <- tm + dts - dt
  fms <- (2 * l - fs * t1 - fe * t2) / (t1 + t2 + 2 * tms)
  list(t1 = t1, t2 = t2, tm = tm, tms = tms, fm = fm, fms = fms, fs = fs, fe = fe, tq = tq, dts = dts)
}

profile_phases <- function(t1, tm, t2, fs, fm, fe) tibble(
  t = c(0, t1, t1, t1 + tm, t1 + tm, t1 + tm + t2),
  f = c(fs, fm, fm, fm, fm, fe),
  phase = rep(c("acc", "const", "dec"), each = 2)
)

plot_clock <- function(q = quantize_block(l = 10, fm = 2, a = 1.6, d = 1.6, fs = 0.3, fe = 0.5, tq = 0.4)) {
  prof <- bind_rows(
    `Nominal` = profile_phases(q$t1, q$tm, q$t2, q$fs, q$fm, q$fe),
    `Rounded to the clock` = profile_phases(q$t1, q$tms, q$t2, q$fs, q$fms, q$fe),
    .id = "which"
  )
  lab <- prof %>%
    group_by(which, phase) %>%
    summarise(t = mean(t), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(label = case_when(
      phase == "acc" ~ "Delta*t[1]", phase == "dec" ~ "Delta*t[2]",
      which == "Nominal" ~ "Delta*t[m]", TRUE ~ "Delta*t[m]^'*'"))
  ggplot(prof, aes(t, f)) +
    geom_area(aes(fill = phase), alpha = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = seq(0, q$dts, by = q$tq), color = "gray55", linewidth = 0.25) +
    geom_text(data = lab, aes(y = -0.22, label = label), parse = TRUE, size = 4) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(acc = "orange", const = "yellowgreen", dec = "orange")) +
    facet_wrap(~which) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.35, 2.1)) +
    labs(x = "t", y = "f")
}

# Look-ahead, one block in curvilinear abscissa, constant acc/dec a:
# fwd: forward step (accelerations only), bwd: backward step (decelerations only),
# final: resulting profile from (s0, vi) to (sf, vf) with nominal feed vm
la_block <- function(vi, vm, vf, sf = 5, a = 15, n = 400) {
  sq <- function(x) sqrt(pmax(x, 0))
  tibble(s = seq(0, sf, length.out = n)) %>%
    mutate(
      acc_vi = sqrt(vi^2 + 2 * a * s),
      dec_vf = sqrt(vf^2 + 2 * a * (sf - s)),
      dec_vi = sq(vi^2 - 2 * a * s),
      acc_vf = sq(vf^2 - 2 * a * (sf - s)),
      fwd = pmin(acc_vi, pmax(vm, acc_vf)),
      bwd = pmin(dec_vf, pmax(vm, dec_vi)),
      final = pmin(acc_vi, dec_vf, pmax(vm, dec_vi, acc_vf))
    )
}

la_plot <- function(vi, vm, vf, sf = 5, a = 15, steps = "fwd", ymax = 11) {
  b <- la_block(vi, vm, vf, sf, a)
  s <- seq(0, 5.5, length.out = 300)
  guides <- bind_rows(
    tibble(s = s, v = sqrt(vi^2 + 2 * a * s), g = "acc_vi"),
    tibble(s = s, v = suppressWarnings(sqrt(vf^2 - 2 * a * (sf - s))), g = "acc_vf"),
    tibble(s = s, v = suppressWarnings(sqrt(-2 * a * (sf - s))), g = "stop")
  ) %>% filter(!is.na(v))
  s1 <- (vm^2 - vi^2) / (2 * a)
  s2 <- sf - (vf^2 - vm^2) / (2 * a)
  lab <- tribble(
    ~s, ~v, ~label, ~hjust,
    0, vi + 0.8, "(s[0]*','~v[i])", -0.1,
    sf, vf + 0.8, "(s[f]*','~v[f])", 1.05,
    sf, 0.6, "(s[f]*','~0)", 1.1
  )
  marks <- tibble(s = c(s1, s2), v = vm, label = c("(s[1]*','~v[m])", "(s[2]*','~v[m])")) %>%
    filter(s > 0, s < sf)
  p <- ggplot(b, aes(x = s)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = vm, linetype = 2, color = "gray40") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = sf, linetype = 2, color = "gray40") +
    geom_line(data = guides, aes(y = v, group = g), linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.3, color = "gray30") +
    geom_line(aes(y = fwd), linewidth = 1.2, color = "firebrick")
  if ("bwd" %in% steps)
    p <- p + geom_line(aes(y = bwd), linewidth = 1.2, color = "forestgreen", linetype = "22")
  p +
    geom_point(data = tibble(s = c(0, sf), v = c(vi, vf)), aes(y = v),
               shape = 4, size = 4, stroke = 1.5, color = "firebrick") +
    geom_point(data = marks, aes(y = v), shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 2.5) +
    geom_text(data = marks, aes(y = v + 0.9, label = label), parse = TRUE, size = 3.6) +
    geom_text(data = lab, aes(y = v, label = label, hjust = hjust), parse = TRUE, size = 3.6) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.5, 5.5), ylim = c(-0.5, ymax), expand = FALSE) +
    labs(x = "s", y = quote(v == dot(s)))
}
```

## CNC kernel tasks

The **CNC kernel** is the part of the CNC controller that implements the **real-time control loop**. It is responsible for:

- Understanding a part-program (parsing)
- Generate velocity profiles (profiling)
- Position interpolation (project trajectoryb on the machine axes)
- Generate command signals (actuation) to the axes drives


::: {.callout-note}
Beside these tasks, the rest of the CNC also takes care of the GUI, programs selection, editing and storing, networking, tables management (presets and tools), interaction with the PLC, and other non-real-time tasks. The CNC kernel is the part of the CNC that is **real-time** and must be implemented in a **real-time operating system** (RTOS)
:::


## Profiling

::::columns
:::column
Profiling is where motion algorithms are implemented. For every block:

- preserve block length: $\displaystyle\int_{t_a}^{t_b} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau = l$
- limit acceleration to the maximum allowed by the machine
- limit jerks, to minimize vibrations and mechanical stress
:::

:::column
```{r}
# toolpath made of 5 blocks, each with its own trapezoidal profile (stop at the corners)
trapz_pts <- function(l, fm = 2, a = 4) {
  t1 <- fm / a
  tm <- l / fm - t1
  tibble(t = c(0, t1, t1 + tm, 2 * t1 + tm), f = c(0, fm, fm, 0))
}
path <- tibble(x = c(0, 3, 7, 8.5, 6, 4.2), y = c(3, 3.8, 3.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.8))
hl <- 3   # highlighted block
prof <- path %>%
  mutate(l = sqrt((lead(x) - x)^2 + (lead(y) - y)^2)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(l)) %>%
  mutate(id = row_number(), tp = map(l, trapz_pts),
         t0 = lag(cumsum(map_dbl(tp, ~ max(.$t))), default = 0)) %>%
  unnest(tp) %>%
  mutate(t = t + t0)
panels <- c("Toolpath (X, Y)", "Feed rate f(t)")
bind_rows(
  path %>% transmute(panel = panels[1], h = x, v = y, id = c(1:5, 5)),
  prof %>% transmute(panel = panels[2], h = t, v = f, id = id)
) %>%
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = panels)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(h, v)) +
  geom_area(data = ~ filter(.x, panel == panels[2], id == hl), fill = "firebrick", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = ~ filter(.x, panel == panels[2]), aes(group = id), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_path(data = ~ filter(.x, panel == panels[1]), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_path(data = ~ filter(.x, panel == panels[1]) %>% slice(hl:(hl + 1)), linewidth = 1.6, color = "firebrick") +
  geom_point(data = ~ filter(.x, panel == panels[1]), size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = tibble(panel = factor(panels[2], levels = panels), h = mean(range(prof$t[prof$id == hl])), v = 2.6),
            label = "integral(f(tau)*d*tau, t[a], t[b]) == l", parse = TRUE, color = "firebrick") +
  geom_blank(data = tibble(panel = factor(panels[2], levels = panels), h = 0, v = 3)) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow=2) +
  labs(x = c("time (s)", "X"), y = NULL)
```
:::
::::


## Profiling

Discrete time-base (clock steps of $t_q$) and feedrate quantization. Block durations must be scaled to a multiple of $t_q$ yet maintaining the same block length. The actual feedrate is reduced accordingly.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| out-width: "792px"
#| out-height: "190px"
#| fig-align: center
plot_clock()
```

$$
\Delta t_1 = \frac{f_m - f_s}{a}, \quad
\Delta t_2 = \frac{f_m - f_e}{d}, \quad
\Delta t_m = \frac{l}{f_m} - \Delta t_1 \frac{f_m + f_s}{2 f_m} - \Delta t_2 \frac{f_e + f_m}{2 f_m}
$$

$$
\Delta t^* = \mathrm{int}\left(\frac{\Delta t}{t_q} + 1\right) t_q = \Delta t_1 + \Delta t_m^* + \Delta t_2, \qquad
\Delta t_m^* = \Delta t_m + \Delta t^* - \Delta t
$$

## Profiling

Discrete time-base (clock steps of $t_q$) and feedrate quantization. Block durations must be scaled to a multiple of $t_q$ yet maintaining the same block length. The actual feedrate is reduced accordingly.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| out-width: "792px"
#| out-height: "190px"
#| fig-align: center
plot_clock()
```

$$
\int_{t_s}^{t_e} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau = \frac{\Delta t_1}{2}(f_m^* + f_s) + \Delta t_m^* f_m^* + \frac{\Delta t_2}{2}(f_m^* + f_e) = l
$$

$$
f_m^* = \frac{2l - f_s \Delta t_1 - f_e \Delta t_2}{\Delta t_1 + \Delta t_2 + 2\Delta t_m^*}, \qquad
a^* = \frac{f_m^* - f_s}{\Delta t_1}, \qquad
d^* = \frac{f_e - f_m^*}{\Delta t_2}
$$

## Profiling

In **short segments** there's no time enough to reach the nominal feedrate:  $\Delta t_m \le 0$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="35%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2.67
#| out-width: "300px"
#| out-height: "200px"
#| fig-align: center
# short block: Delta t_m <= 0, the feed never reaches f_m
a <- 1.6; d <- 1.2; l <- 3
t1 <- sqrt(2 * l / (a + a^2 / d)); t2 <- a / d * t1
tibble(t = c(0, t1, t1, t1 + t2), f = c(0, a * t1, a * t1, 0), phase = rep(c("acc", "dec"), each = 2)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(t, f)) +
  geom_area(aes(fill = phase), alpha = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = seq(0, 3.2, by = 0.2), color = "gray55", linewidth = 0.25) +
  annotate("text", x = c(t1 / 2, t1 + t2 / 2), y = 0.4, label = c("Delta*t[1]", "Delta*t[2]"), parse = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(acc = "orange", dec = "yellowgreen")) +
  labs(x = "t", y = "f")
```
:::
::: {.column width="65%"}
$$
\int_{t_s}^{t_e} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau = \frac{a\Delta t_1^2 + d\Delta t_2^2}{2}; \quad a\Delta t_1 = d\Delta t_2
$$

$$
\frac{\Delta t_1^2 (a + a^2/d)}{2} = l
$$
:::
::::

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta t_1 &= \sqrt{\frac{2l}{a + a^2/d}} \\
\Delta t_2 &= \frac{a}{d}\Delta t_1 \\
\Delta t_2^* &= \Delta t^* - \Delta t_1
\end{aligned}
\qquad
f_m^*(\Delta t_1 + \Delta t_2^*) = 2l
\qquad
\begin{aligned}
a^* &= \frac{f_m^* - f_s}{\Delta t_1} \\
d^* &= \frac{f_e - f_m^*}{\Delta t_2^*}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Motion interpolation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
- The speed profile is evaluated and integrated at each time tick: $\lambda(t) = 1/L\int_0^t f(\tau)\,d\tau$
- The axes set-points are calculated with the parametric equation of the path
- For a **linear motion**:

$$
\begin{aligned}
X(t) &= X_0 + \Delta X \lambda(t) \\
Y(t) &= Y_0 + \Delta Y \lambda(t) \\
Z(t) &= Z_0 + \Delta Z \lambda(t)
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 3.6
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "310px"
#| out-height: "431px"
#| fig-align: center
# feed profile and normalised curvilinear abscissa lambda(t) = s(t) / l
t1 <- 1; tm <- 2; t2 <- 1
tibble(t = seq(0, t1 + tm + t2, length.out = 400)) %>%
  mutate(`f(t)` = pmin(t / t1, 1, (t1 + tm + t2 - t) / t2),
         `lambda(t)` = cumsum(`f(t)`) / sum(`f(t)`)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-t) %>%
  ggplot(aes(t, value)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(t1, t1 + tm), linetype = 2, color = "gray40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y", labeller = label_parsed, strip.position = "left") +
  labs(x = "t (s)", y = NULL) +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside")
```
:::
::::

## Motion interpolation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
For **arc interpolation**:

$$
\begin{aligned}
X(t) &= X_c + R\cos(\vartheta_0 + \Delta\vartheta \lambda(t)) \\
Y(t) &= Y_c + R\sin(\vartheta_0 + \Delta\vartheta \lambda(t)) \\
Z(t) &= Z_0 + \Delta Z \lambda(t)
\end{aligned}
$$

Warning: feedrate may be reduced

$$
f_{m,a} = \min\left(f_m, \sqrt{aR}\right)
$$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images-1/arc-diagram.svg){fig-align="center" height=330}
:::
::::

## Motion interpolation

Two alternative G-code syntax for arcs:

- arch center: `G[02|03] X[`$X_f$`] Y[`$Y_f$`] I[`$I$`] J[`$J$`]`
- radius: `G[02|03] X[`$X_f$`] Y[`$Y_f$`] R[`$\pm R$`]` (radius sign discriminates which arc to take)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](images-1/arc-syntax.svg){fig-align="center" height=280}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_0 &= \cos^{-1} I/R \\
\vartheta_f &= \cos^{-1} (X_f - X_c)/R \\
X_c &= X_0 + I \\
Y_c &= Y_0 + J \\
R &= \sqrt{I^2 + J^2} \\
R^2 &= (X_f - X_c)^2 + (Y_f - Y_c)^2
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
::::

## Motion interpolation

**Center coordinates** (two alternatives depending on the sign of $R$)

$$
\Delta x = X_f - X_0, \qquad \Delta y = Y_f - Y_0
$$

$$
X_c = X_0 + \frac{1}{2}\left(\Delta x - \mathrm{sign}(R)\,\frac{\sqrt{-\Delta y^2 (\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2)(-4R^2 + \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2)}}{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}\right)
$$

$$
Y_c = Y_0 + \frac{\Delta y}{2} + \mathrm{sign}(R)\,\frac{\Delta x \sqrt{-\Delta y^2 (\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2)(-4R^2 + \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2)}}{2\Delta x^2 \Delta y + 2\Delta y^3}
$$

## Jerk

:::: columns
::: column
Jerk-limited profiling: 

* corners in feedrate imply discontinuous acceleration
* discontinuous acceleration mean **infinite jerk**
* infinite jerk produces vibrations and mechanical stress
* for **limited jerk profiling** each segment is split into 7 ranges (vs. 3)
:::

:::column
```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: "654px"
#| out-height: "430px"
#| fig-align: center
# jerk-limited profile: 7 phases (jerk +j, 0, -j, cruise, -j, 0, +j)
fm <- 1; amax <- 1; j <- 4; tm <- 1; dt <- 0.001
tj <- amax / j; ta <- fm / amax - tj
phases <- c(tj, ta, tj, tm, tj, ta, tj)
jerk <- c(j, 0, -j, 0, -j, 0, j)
bounds <- cumsum(c(0, phases))
tibble(t = seq(0, sum(phases), by = dt)) %>%
  mutate(j = jerk[findInterval(t, bounds, rightmost.closed = TRUE)],
         a = cumsum(j) * dt, f = cumsum(a) * dt) %>%
  pivot_longer(-t) %>%
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = c("f", "a", "j"), labels = c("f", "a", "dot(a)"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(t, value)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bounds, linetype = 2, color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y", labeller = label_parsed, strip.position = "left") +
  labs(x = "t (s)", y = NULL) +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside")
```
:::
::::

## Look-ahead feedrate profile

The above presented algorithm assumes that the instant speed goes to zero at each corner. This is not acceptable in real CNC machines, for two reasons:

- **Problem 1:** tangent or semi-tangent blocks would result in excessive reduction of feedrate wrt nominal
- **Problem 2:** it shall be possible to accelerate to nominal feedrate with continuous acceleration over $n$ short segments, and it may take more than one segment to decelerate down to stop

To solve these issue we need to plan the velocity profile **across multiple blocks** of G-Code. This is called **look-ahead**

## Look-ahead feedrate profile

Approach:

1. Calculate $v_i$, $v_m$, $v_f$ for each block, considering $v = v(s)$
2. Forward step: from block 1 to block $n$, calculate accelerations only
3. Backward step: from block $n$ to block 1, calculate decelerations only and compose with accelerations
4. Change variable $s \to t$ and get $v = v(t)$
5. Reshape $v^* = \dfrac{v(t)}{k}$, where $k = t_f / t_f^*$ and $t_f^*$ is the multiple of $t_q$ immediately larger than the total time $t_f$ (block by block)

## Constant Acc/Dec

- We cannot calculate feed profiles in time abscissa, for we don't know the duration of each step
- Thus we start planning in **curvilinear abscissa** $s$:
  - $s(t) = s_0 + v_0 t + a t^2/2$, and thus $t(s) = \dfrac{1}{a}\left(-v_0 \pm \sqrt{2a(s - s_0) + v_0^2}\right)$
  - Since $v(t(s)) = v_0 + a\, t(s)$, it follows that $v(s) = \sqrt{2a(s - s_0) + v_0^2}$
  - So accelerations and decelerations follow a square root law of $s$
- In jerk-limited approach, we'd have a cubic root branch at the beginning and at the end of each acc/dec branch

## Look-ahead feedrate

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
Step 1: calculate velocities:

- $v_{i,i} = v_{f,i-1}$, or 0 for first sg.
- $v_{m,i} = f_i$ for G01
- $v_m = \min(f_i, \sqrt{aR})$ for G02/G03
- $v_{f,i} = \dfrac{v_{m,i} + v_{m,i+1}}{2}\cos\alpha_i$
- $v_{f,i} = 0$ for last segment or if $v_{m,i} = 0$
:::
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
# blocks: length, nominal feed and angle with the next block (deg)
blk <- tibble(l = c(5, 5, 3, 11, 6, 1, 1), f = c(8, 8, 7, 3, 7, 7, 7), alpha = c(40, 10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 90)) %>%
  mutate(s0 = lag(cumsum(l), default = 0), s1 = cumsum(l),
         vf = if_else(row_number() == n(), 0, (f + lead(f)) / 2 * cos(alpha * pi / 180)),
         vf = pmin(vf, f, lead(f, default = 0)))
first <- la_block(0, blk$f[1], blk$vf[1], sf = blk$l[1])
ggplot(blk) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = s0, xend = s1, y = f, yend = f), linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = s1, xend = s1, y = 0, yend = pmax(f, lead(f, default = 0))), linetype = 3) +
  geom_line(data = first, aes(s, final), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_point(data = bind_rows(tibble(s1 = 0, vf = 0), blk), aes(s1, vf), color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "s", y = quote(v == dot(s)))
```
:::
::::

## Forward step: accelerations

Long segments, $v_i < v_m$:

A. $v_f > v_m$, $s_0 < s_1 < s_2 < s_f$

B. $v_f < v_m$, $s_0 < s_1 < s_f < s_2$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "520px"
#| out-height: "355px"
la_plot(1, 8, 9)
```

## Forward step: accelerations

Long segments, $v_i > v_m$:

A. $v_f > v_m$, $s_1 < s_0 < s_2 < s_f$

B. $v_f < v_m$, $s_1 < s_0 < s_f < s_2$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4.4

```

## Forward step: accelerations {.smaller}

Short segments:

- $s_0 < s_f < s_1$
- $v_f$ and $s_2$ are not relevant

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 4.4
```

## Change of variable

### Back to time abscissa
Convert back **from curvilinear abscissa to time**, one block at a time:

* Calculate $v(t) = v_0 + at$, $s(t) = s_0 + v_0 t + at^2/2$ in the ranges $[s_i, s_1]$, $[s_1, s_2]$, $[s_2, s_f]$
* Calculate timings $t_1$, $t_2$, $t_f$

### Reshape for discrete time

- Calculate $t_f^* = \lceil t_f / t_q + 1 \rceil t_q$
- Calculate $k = t_f^* / t_f$
- **Rescale feedrate** so that $v^*(t) = \dfrac{v(t)}{k}$

## Receding horizon

- This algorithm requires a sequence of blocks starting and ending at zero feedrate
- You can assume that `G00` blocks mark full stops at corners
- Nonetheless, a program can consist in thousands of sequential G01/G02/G03 blocks: memory problem
- **Solution:**
  - At run time, pre-elaborate a buffer made of a limited number of blocks (say 100) assuming the last one stops (look-ahead buffer)
  - Re-calculate the moving buffer as soon as a block is done by adding a new block at the end (FIFO): start backward (dec) until no change, then forward (acc)
  - The buffer size depends on available memory and on computation time (must be shorter than the time needed to execute the buffer); calculations are done in parallel in a separate thread

## Machining error sources

::::columns
:::{.column width="34%"}
* [Process error sources]{.bgreen}: tool/workpiece interaction (minimized by proper process conditions)
* **Structural error sources**: time-dependent, eventually become stable and can be compensated
* [Machine error sources]{.bblue}: more difficult to compensate, potentially ever changing
:::

:::{.column width="66%"}

## Error Compensation (A5)

Compensating for error means to **measure errors** and to **apply corrections** to the machine tool commands. This is a **closed-loop control** approach

* Adaptive control systems (A/C) = **evaluation** attribute (A5)
* Factors under evaluation:
  - forces/deflections
  - machining errors
  - **thermoelastic** dilatations/deformations

## Profiling errors

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
Look-ahead can alter trajectory, especially at corners:

- More evident at high speed
- When a sharp corner is needed, use curls or disable look-ahead
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
# 90-degree corner at constant feed, each axis follows its command with a first-order lag (Kv)
corner <- function(feed, Kv = 40, dt = 1e-4, L = 2) {
  v <- feed / 60
  t <- seq(0, 2 * L / v + 0.2, by = dt)
  xc <- 40 + pmin(v * t - L, 0)
  yc <- -10 + pmax(v * t - L, 0)
  xa <- ya <- numeric(length(t))
  xa[1] <- xc[1] - v / Kv; ya[1] <- yc[1]
  for (i in 2:length(t)) {
    xa[i] <- xa[i - 1] + Kv * (xc[i - 1] - xa[i - 1]) * dt
    ya[i] <- ya[i - 1] + Kv * (yc[i - 1] - ya[i - 1]) * dt
  }
  e <- min(sqrt((xa - 40)^2 + (ya + 10)^2))
  tibble(x = xa, y = ya, F = sprintf("%d mm/min (error %.2f mm)", feed, e))
}
bind_rows(corner(500), corner(1500)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, y, color = F)) +
  geom_path(data = tibble(x = c(39.5, 40, 40), y = c(-10, -10, -9.5)), color = "black", linetype = 2) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 1) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(39.5, 40.1), ylim = c(-10.1, -9.5)) +
  labs(x = "X (mm)", y = "Y (mm)", color = "Feed rate") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")
```

## Elementary errors

- Three linear errors per axis (linearity, straightness, undulation)
- Three angular errors per axis (roll, pitch, yaw)
- Two squareness errors between axes 1 and 2
- Two squareness errors between axes 3 and 2
- Total of 18 + 4 = 22 elementary errors, 18 of which are position-dependent

## Calibration

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: "100%"
# simulated calibration of a 200 mm axis: 5 runs, measured every 10 mm
set.seed(1)
xs <- seq(0, 200, by = 10)
shape <- 1.5 * sin(xs / 25) + 0.8 * sin(xs / 9 + 1)
expand_grid(run = 1:5, x = xs) %>%
  mutate(straightness = shape[match(x, xs)] + rnorm(n(), sd = 0.6)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, straightness)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = run), color = "gray60") +
  geom_point(color = "gray40", size = 1) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = ~ tibble(ymin = mean(.x) - 2 * sd(.x), ymax = mean(.x) + 2 * sd(.x)),
               geom = "ribbon", alpha = 0.15, fill = "firebrick") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Axis position (mm)", y = "Straightness (µm)", title = "Straightness residuals")
expand_grid(run = 1:5, dir = c("forward", "backward"), x = xs) %>%
  mutate(error = 0.025 * x + 0.8 * sin(x / 30) + if_else(dir == "forward", 1.2, -1.2) + rnorm(n(), sd = 0.3)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, error, color = dir)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Nominal position (mm)", y = "Positioning error (µm)", color = NULL,
       title = "Linearity (positioning) error") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
